Love: the learner shares the available materials while exploring and making a collage in Creative Arts and Sports.

skills.name: Name the categories of Creative Arts and Sports and how they relate
skills.mastery: The child names the categories (art and craft, music, physical education and sports, and performing arts such as drama and dance) and says they work together, for example music with dance and drama. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G7.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) make a collage on the categories of the Creative Arts and Sports.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Naming elements of music in a song (Grade 6) is one category met before all are named. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
Painting and collage (Grade 6) are examples of the visual arts category. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the categories never work together, so music has nothing to do with dance or drama.

example.question: How do music and dance relate?

misconceptions.cause: Each category is taught in its own lesson, so the child sees them as separate subjects.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They never go together" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Watch a folk dance: name the music, the movement and the costume, three categories in one.
misconceptions.feedback: Music and dance often work together.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves physical education and sports out of the subject and names an unrelated subject instead.

example.question: Which is a category of Creative Arts and Sports?

misconceptions.cause: Until Grade 6 PE was a separate lesson, so the child does not expect it in Creative Arts.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mathematics" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Read the subject name aloud: Creative Arts and Sports. List what PE adds.
misconceptions.feedback: Physical education and sports is a category.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only painting is art and craft, putting football there because it is creative.

example.question: Which is art and craft?

misconceptions.cause: The child uses "creative" to mean any fun activity.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Playing football" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Sort ten activities into visual arts, performing arts and sports with the reason for each.
misconceptions.feedback: A collage is art and craft.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts drama under sports because both are performed in front of people.

example.question: Which category does drama belong to?

misconceptions.cause: Both drama and sport have an audience and a stage or field.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sports" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the performer does: tells a story (performing arts) or competes (sport).
misconceptions.feedback: Drama tells a story to an audience. It is a performing art.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says setting is the people.

example.question: What is the setting of a story?

misconceptions.cause: Characters are the first thing the child notices in a story, so "setting" gets their meaning.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The people in it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Ask "where and when?" for three stories and underline the answers.
misconceptions.feedback: The setting is the place and time.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says characters are the place.

example.question: Who are the characters?
example.correct_answer: The people or animals in it

misconceptions.cause: The child swaps two new words learnt in the same lesson.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The place of the story" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Ask "who?" for characters and "where?" for setting with one story.
misconceptions.feedback: Characters are the people or animals in the story.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says plot is the title.

example.question: What is the plot?

misconceptions.cause: The title is at the top and seems to sum up the story, so the child calls it the plot.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The title of the story" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Retell a story in three events: that chain is the plot.
misconceptions.feedback: The plot is the order of events.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes agility with flexibility.

example.question: Which is the ability to change direction quickly?

misconceptions.cause: Both agility and flexibility sound like being good at moving.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Flexibility" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Do a zigzag run (agility) and a sit-and-reach (flexibility); name each.
misconceptions.feedback: Agility is changing direction quickly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes flexibility with strength.

example.question: Which is the range of movement at a joint?

misconceptions.cause: A flexible person can lift a leg high, which the child sees as strength.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Strength" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Compare touching the toes (flexibility) with lifting a heavy bag (strength).
misconceptions.feedback: Flexibility is the range of movement at a joint.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes endurance with speed.

example.question: Which is lasting a long time without tiring?

misconceptions.cause: Fast runners win races, so the child thinks speed is what lasts.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Speed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Compare a 60 m sprint (speed) with a 1,500 m run (endurance).
misconceptions.feedback: Endurance is lasting a long time without tiring.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives a minim one beat, taking it for a crotchet.

example.question: How many beats is a minim?

misconceptions.cause: The minim and the crotchet both have a stem; only the hollow head differs.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "1" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Draw both: hollow head and stem is the minim, two beats; filled head is the crotchet, one.
misconceptions.feedback: A minim is 2 beats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives a semibreve two beats, taking it for a minim.

example.question: How many beats is a semibreve?

misconceptions.cause: Both have hollow heads; the child does not notice the semibreve has no stem.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "2" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Line up semibreve, minim, crotchet and count 4, 2, 1 while clapping.
misconceptions.feedback: A semibreve is 4 beats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts four crotchet beats in a bar of two-four time, reading the lower 4 as the count.

example.question: In 2 time, a bar holds how many crotchet beats?

misconceptions.cause: The child reads the bottom number of 2/4 as the number of beats.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "4" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: The top number counts the beats: 2/4 has two crotchet beats in a bar.
misconceptions.feedback: A bar in 2 time holds 2 crotchet beats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the spaces for the lines.

example.question: What are the lines of the treble staff from the bottom?

misconceptions.cause: FACE is the easiest rhyme to remember, so the child uses it for everything.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "F A C E" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Lines: Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit. Spaces: FACE.
misconceptions.feedback: The lines are E G B D F.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the lines for the spaces.

example.question: What are the spaces of the treble staff from the bottom?

misconceptions.cause: The child learnt both rhymes and swaps them.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "E G B D F" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Point at a space: FACE fits in the spaces.
misconceptions.feedback: The spaces are F A C E.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names the bottom line of the treble staff F, starting FACE on a line.

example.question: Which note is on the bottom line of the treble staff?

misconceptions.cause: The child starts FACE at the bottom of the staff, not in the first space.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "F" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Count up from the bottom line: E (line), F (space), G (line).
misconceptions.feedback: The bottom line is E.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says the theme of a story is its title.

example.question: What is the theme of a story?
example.correct_answer: the main idea or lesson it is about

misconceptions.cause: The title is the first words and seems to say what the story is about.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "its title" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Read a fable: the title names the animals, the theme is the lesson.
misconceptions.feedback: The theme is the main idea or lesson, not the title.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks muscular strength is the same as being big.

example.question: What is muscular strength?
example.correct_answer: the force a muscle can produce

misconceptions.cause: Strong people in films are often big.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "being big" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a small learner lifting a heavy load with a big learner who cannot.
misconceptions.feedback: Muscular strength is the force a muscle can produce, not body size.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives a single quaver one whole beat.

example.question: How long is one quaver in two-four time?

misconceptions.cause: Each quaver has its own stem and flag, so the child counts it as a whole note.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "one beat" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap ta-te: two quavers share one beat.
misconceptions.feedback: One quaver lasts half a beat. Two quavers make one beat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names the note on the ledger line below the treble staff D.

example.question: Which note sits on one ledger line below the treble staff?

misconceptions.cause: The child counts down from E but forgets the space below is D and the ledger line is C.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "D" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count down: E line, D space, C ledger line.
misconceptions.feedback: One ledger line below the treble staff is middle C.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

skills.name: Tell how balance works in a picture
skills.mastery: The child says balance is the even spread of visual weight in a picture, and names symmetrical (both sides alike), asymmetrical (different but equal in weight) and radial (spreading from the centre) balance. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G7.RUBRIC.2.1, CREA.G7.RUBRIC.2.2, CREA.G7.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: b) draw a picture to apply balance.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Lines of symmetry (Grade 4 Maths) explain symmetrical balance. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
Arranging a still life (Grade 6) is arranging for balance. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

skills.name: Tell warm colours from cool colours
skills.mastery: The child says red, orange and yellow are warm colours (like fire and sun) and blue, green and violet are cool (like water and sky), and says warm colours seem to come forward. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G7.RUBRIC.2.1, CREA.G7.RUBRIC.2.2, CREA.G7.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: d) paint a scenery based on colour temperature.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Warm and cool colours were first sorted on the Grade 6 colour wheel. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.
A wash for the sky (Grade 5) is where cool colours are used. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher.

misconceptions.error: Says symmetrical balance has two different sides, swapping it with asymmetrical.

example.question: What is symmetrical balance?

misconceptions.cause: Symmetrical and asymmetrical sound alike.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Both sides are different" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Fold a butterfly drawing: both halves match, so symmetrical.
misconceptions.feedback: Symmetrical balance has both sides alike.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks balance means making every part the same colour.

example.question: What is balance in a picture?

misconceptions.cause: The child links balance with sameness.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Making everything the same colour" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Show a big shape balanced by two small ones of the same visual weight.
misconceptions.feedback: Balance is the even spread of visual weight.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Picks "items in a straight line" for radial balance.

example.question: What is radial balance?

misconceptions.cause: The child has not met "radius", so radial means nothing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Items in a straight line" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Show a sunflower or a wheel: parts spread out from the centre.
misconceptions.feedback: Radial balance spreads from the centre.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts blue among warm colours.

example.question: Which is a warm colour?

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of colours they like as warm.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Blue" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Sort colours by fire (warm) and water (cool).
misconceptions.feedback: Red, orange and yellow are warm.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts red among cool colours.

example.question: Which is a cool colour?

misconceptions.cause: Red is a strong colour, and the child mixes strong with cool.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Red" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Hold red near a picture of fire and blue near water.
misconceptions.feedback: Blue, green and violet are cool.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes the feeling of warm and cool.

example.question: Which colours remind us of the sun and fire?

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard "cool" used to mean good.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cool colours" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the sun looks like: red, orange, yellow are warm.
misconceptions.feedback: Warm colours remind us of sun and fire.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a picture is only balanced if the main object is in the exact centre.

example.question: Can a picture be balanced with the main tree on the left?
example.wrong_answer: no, it must be in the centre
example.correct_answer: yes, if something on the right balances its weight

misconceptions.cause: The child knows only symmetrical balance.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it must be in the centre" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Balance a big tree on the left with a house and a bird on the right.
misconceptions.feedback: A picture can be balanced off-centre if the weight on each side is equal. That is asymmetrical balance.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Paints far hills in warm red, so they jump forward.

example.question: Which colours make hills look far away?

misconceptions.cause: The child picks bright colours to make things noticed.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "warm colours" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Paint two strips of hills, warm and cool; which looks further?
misconceptions.feedback: Cool colours seem to go back, so far hills are painted blue.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: watch live/recorded narration clips to discuss storytelling techniques (use of voice, use of body, use of songs, audience involvement, props and costumes),
explore to identify a pertinent and contemporary issue in society for storytelling,
develop, in groups, a character/characters for a story,
arrange milestones in a sequential order (beginning, middle and end) to create a short story,
draw a sequence of a moving character to create a flip book animation focussing on;(sequencing of objects/image(s), positioning of objects on subsequent pages, creativity (storyline),
finish and present the flip book with focus on: craftsmanship in use of materials and tools, - collating the papers, binding of papers (using string/stapling,
riffle the flip book by emphasising on; frequency of image(s), speed of flick per second to animate the story,
perform a vocal and physical warm up exercises in readiness for storytelling,
rehearse the short story for performance,
perform a short story to an audience,
record the narration and avail it on a digital platform.
key_inquiry_questions: How can storytelling be made interesting?
How can flip book animation be used in storytelling?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication: the learner speaks clearly and engagingly during class discussions and when performing stories.
Collaboration: the learner contributes to group activities when creating and performing stories.
Self-efficacy: In performing a story, the learner builds confidence and self-esteem.
Learning to Learn: the learner is equipped with concepts, knowledge, and skills relevant for continued learning and life.
Digital literacy: the learner interacts with ICT gadgets to research and watch digital content relating to narratives and film book animation.
sub_strands.values:
Respect: the learner accommodates others’ views when creating and performing the short story.
Peace: the learner works in harmony with others during the rehearsal sessions and performance.
Integrity: the learner is equipped with the value of honesty through creation of own original works devoid of plagiarism.
Unity: the learner works in groups when creating and performing stories.
sub_strands.pcis:
Social Cohesion: the learner acquires group cohesion skills while working with other team members.
Life skills education: the learner gains communication skills through performances of stories.
Career guidance: the learner derives skills in the preparation of costumes and props from locally available materials and technology.
sub_strands.links:
English and Kiswahili: the learner takes part in class discussions using these languages as a medium of communication.
Indigenous Languages: the learner uses these languages as a medium of communication as they interact with some resource persons from the community.
Social Science: the learner explores social science concepts by narrating stories that reflect different historical periods, cultural practices, or societal issues.

Folk song performing techniques- (voice projection and balance, phrasing, tempo, tone, dynamics, expression and interpretation, gestures and movement, intensity, mood, idiom/authenticity)
learning_experiences: brainstorm to classify the folk songs,
visit an actual or virtual cultural centre to watch and select a solo or group folk song from any Kenyan community for performance,
take a role in performing a solo or group folk song applying performance techniques
key_inquiry_questions: What is the role of folk songs in Kenyan society?
How can performances of Kenyan folk songs be made interesting?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Citizenship: by performing folk songs from different Kenyan cultures, the learner recognizes and appreciates cultural diversity in Kenya, thus fostering a sense of shared responsibility in preserving and promoting cultural heritage.
Critical thinking: is demonstrated as the learner interprets the significance of each component in a folk song, fostering a deeper understanding of cultural and musical expressions.
Learning to Learn: is enhanced as the learner researches and adapts folk song performance and costume decoration techniques, demonstrating an openness to new ideas and methods.
Creativity and Imagination: the learner explores and combines unique techniques in decorating the costumes by stencil printing, and selecting songs and materials for performance,
Digital literacy is developed when the learner explores digital platforms to research, document and share folk song performances.
Communication and Collaboration: are honed as the learner speaks articulately and interacts with others toexecute various components of folk songs.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: expressed as the learner collaborates with others to improvise costumes, collect found materials, rehearse and perform folk song as a shared cultural experience.
Patriotism: is encouraged as the learner showcases a pride in presenting the folk song, contributing to the celebration and recognition of Kenyan cultural heritage,
Integrity: is demonstrated as the learner improvises and decorates costumes that ensure authenticity and decency, and acknowledges the origin of the songs during the folk songs’ presentations,
Respect is demonstrated as the learner performs and appreciates folksongs from diverse Kenyan cultures, thus recognizing the diversity in performance technique and musical expression.
sub_strands.pcis:
Citizenship Education: the learner performs folk songs whose content promotes cultural awareness.
Social Awareness: the learner understands the existence of folks songs as a means of cultural expression and encounters new themes and content while searching for and performing folk songs from different Kenyan communities,
sub_strands.links:
Social Studies: Classification of Folk songs involves understanding the cultural and social context of different Kenyan communities, linking to social science.
Languages (English, Kiswahili): Describing and communicating the ideas for costume improvisation requires effective communication skills, linking to language arts components in both English and Kiswahili.

misconceptions.error: Analyses a performance only with "I liked it", giving no evidence.

example.question: Which is an analysis of a folk song?
example.correct_answer: The soloist and chorus answer each other, showing it is a work song sung in a group

misconceptions.cause: The child confuses giving an opinion with analysing.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "I liked it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.

example.wrong_answer: the hare tricked the hyena and ran away

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the hare tricked the hyena and ran away" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask "what is the story teaching?" after retelling.

misconceptions.error: Names a folk song's type only from how fast it is.

example.question: A fast song is sung while winnowing. What type is it?
example.wrong_answer: a dance song, because it is fast

misconceptions.cause: The child uses tempo alone.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a dance song, because it is fast" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Look at the occasion and the words first.
misconceptions.feedback: A song's type comes from its occasion and words, not only its speed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names what the story is about when asked for a storytelling technique.

example.question: Name a technique the storyteller used.
example.correct_answer: changing her voice for each animal

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes the content with how it was told.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a story about a lion" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask "how did she tell it?" not "what was it about?".
misconceptions.feedback: A technique is how the story is told, such as voice changes or pauses.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Arts and Sports teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
